headline: Fed holds at 3.5–3.75% but three officials dissented for a hike, sending the 30-year Treasury yield to its highest level in 19 years and dragging equities sharply lower into the close.
stance: The overnight takeaway: a hawkish hold. Chair Warsh kept rates unchanged but offered no forward guidance and made clear the Fed has no soft inflation target — the bond market heard it as a warning shot, not a reprieve. The 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.21%, its highest since 2007, even as the 2-year fell slightly — the curve is steepening for the wrong reasons (inflation fear, not growth hope). Today's session pivots on AAPL and AMZN earnings after the close and whether Brent crude — which entered a new price extreme yesterday — stays elevated as Iran diplomacy remains stalled.

news.head: Fed holds, hawks dissent
news.body: The FOMC left its benchmark rate at 3.5%–3.75% for the fifth straight meeting, but Cleveland's Hammack, Minneapolis's Kashkari, and Dallas's Logan all voted for an immediate quarter-point hike — the most dissents since September 2016.

news.head: 30-year yield at 19-year high
news.body: After Warsh's press conference, the 30-year Treasury yield surged 12 basis points to 5.21% — its highest level since 2007 — as investors concluded the Fed is behind the curve on inflation; the 10-year settled at a prior cash-close of 4.67% (up 7bps on the day).

news.head: Stocks sold off hard
news.body: The Dow fell roughly 1,153 points and the S&P 500 dropped about 1% after Warsh's remarks; the SPX prior cash close stands at 7,316.15 and the NDX at 24,442.94.

news.head: Iran: Hormuz diplomacy stalls
news.body: Tehran rejected Oman's proposal for joint regional management of the Strait of Hormuz, dashing hopes for de-escalation and keeping an upward floor under energy prices.

news.head: Brent crude new extreme
news.body: Brent crude reached a prior cash close of $90.54/bbl — its first session at an 'elevated' 3-year price extreme — while WTI settled at $84.60/bbl; both spiked sharply Wednesday on Trump's retaliation warning against Iran.

news.head: AAPL & AMZN due after bell
news.body: Apple (consensus EPS $1.88–$1.89, revenue ~$108.9B) and Amazon (consensus EPS $1.81, revenue ~$196.5B) both report tonight; capex guidance and AI-spend commentary are the swing factors after Alphabet's elevated spending alarmed investors earlier this month.

news.head: MSFT & META reported last night
news.body: Microsoft and Meta reported after Wednesday's close; results and management commentary on AI capital expenditure plans will shape pre-market tone for the Nasdaq this morning.

implications: Three dissents signal that the path of least resistance for rates is still higher, not lower — a September hike is a live risk and bond investors are pricing it aggressively into the long end of the curve.
Steep curve via rising long yields without Fed easing is a margin compression signal for equities: it raises the discount rate on future earnings while borrowing costs for companies stay elevated.
Stalled Iran diplomacy keeps a geopolitical risk premium embedded in Brent crude, which feeds directly into inflation expectations (10-year breakeven: 2.26%) and complicates the Fed's ability to cut.

Real rates at 2.41% remain a stiff headwind for growth and tech multiples; the equity risk premium (ERP) is already negative at -2%, meaning Treasuries offer better risk-adjusted returns than stocks on this reading — a structural caution.

Positioning: Speculators just moved to a newly extended long on S&P 500 futures (85th percentile, NEW this week) — speculators are heavily positioned on the long side, a contrarian warning at these levels. Simultaneously, speculators are now at an extended short on VIX futures (10th percentile, NEW this week) — they have almost no bullish bets left on volatility, which is a contrarian floor for the VIX and a warning that complacency in the options market may unwind quickly if earnings disappoint.

watch.head: AAPL & AMZN after close
watch.body: Apple and Amazon report tonight — capex guidance and any commentary on tariff or supply-chain impact from Middle East tensions will determine whether the Nasdaq can recoup Wednesday's losses.

watch.head: 30-year yield — 5.25% resistance
watch.body: The 30-year Treasury yield is at its highest since 2007; a sustained push above 5.25% would tighten financial conditions further and put additional pressure on rate-sensitive sectors including real estate and utilities.

watch.head: Brent crude & Hormuz headlines
watch.body: With Tehran having rejected the latest diplomatic framework, any new strike activity or tanker incident in the Strait of Hormuz could push Brent — already at a fresh price extreme — sharply higher, re-igniting the inflation-fear loop.

watch.head: Jackson Hole (Aug) — Warsh signal
watch.body: The next FOMC meeting is Sep 15–16, but Warsh is expected to speak at Jackson Hole in August; his remarks there will be the market's first real read on whether the committee is tilting toward a September hike.

watch.head: VIX complacency risk
watch.body: The VIX closed at 20.66 (prior cash close) and speculators are newly extended short on VIX futures — if big-tech earnings disappoint tonight, that short-volatility positioning could unwind rapidly, amplifying any equity move lower.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: Fed funds rate held at 3.5%–3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting; three FOMC members (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) dissented in favor of an immediate 25bps hike — the most dissents since 2016.

The 10-year Treasury yield settled at a prior cash close of 4.67%, up 7 basis points on the day; the 30-year surged 12bps to 5.21% — its highest level since 2007 — while the 2-year dipped 4bps to 4.22%.

The yield curve (2s/10s, the gap between short and long rates) sits at 45bps (prior close) — it is steepening as long yields rise faster than short ones, driven by inflation fear rather than growth optimism.
Real rates (the inflation-adjusted cost of borrowing) stand at 2.41% — a high reading that acts as a brake on business investment and asset valuations.
10-year inflation expectations (breakeven) are 2.26%, sitting above the Fed's 2% target; Tehran's rejection of a Hormuz diplomatic framework keeps upside risk to energy-driven inflation alive.

Bond-market stress gauges are calm: the MOVE index (bond volatility, analogous to VIX for stocks) is 74.2 (prior close) and FRA-OIS / SOFR-OIS spreads (a measure of bank-to-bank lending stress — near zero means banks trust each other) are each just 2bps — no credit-crunch signal yet.

Financial conditions overall remain loose: the Chicago Fed's conditions indexes (ANFCI: -0.56, STLFSI: -0.83) are both below zero, meaning money is still easy to borrow relative to history — the rate-hike risk is forward-looking, not yet realized in the plumbing.
sections.positioning: Speculators have almost no bullish bets left on 3-month interest rate futures (SOFR, 4th percentile over 3 years, extended short for 14 weeks) — a standing contrarian-bullish lean on short-term rates, though this is background context, not a new development this week.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Prior cash closes: S&P 500 at 7,316.15, Nasdaq 100 at 24,442.94, Dow at 51,594.14 — all fell sharply after Warsh's press conference Wednesday.

Market breadth was solid before the Fed: 71.4% of S&P 500 stocks were above their 50-day moving average and 73.7% above their 200-day average (as of Jul 28), but a hawkish-hold reaction could dent those readings today.

The Nasdaq 100 shows narrower breadth: only 50.5% of its stocks are above their 50-day moving average (vs. 68.3% above the 200-day), signaling that recent strength has been concentrated in a handful of large names.

CAPE (the long-run price-to-earnings ratio that smooths out business cycles) sits at 39.93 — historically stretched; the equity risk premium is -2%, meaning broad equities are priced to deliver less than Treasuries on a risk-adjusted basis.
The equity-credit correlation is 0.684 (prior close) — stocks and credit spreads are moving closely together, so any widening in credit markets would amplify equity pressure.

SKEW index at 139.6 (prior close) — options traders are paying elevated prices to hedge against a big market drop, suggesting sophisticated investors are cautious even if the VIX headline number looks moderate.

Apple and Amazon report after today's close; capex guidance is the single biggest swing factor for the Nasdaq given investor sensitivity to AI-infrastructure spending following Alphabet's earlier raise.
sections.positioning: Speculators are newly extended long on S&P 500 futures (85th percentile of 3-year range, NEW this week) — speculators are heavily positioned on the long side, a contrarian warning. Simultaneously, speculators moved to an extended short on VIX futures (10th percentile, NEW this week) — they have almost no bullish bets left on volatility, which is a contrarian floor for the VIX. Together these two new extremes suggest the options and futures market is priced for calm, making it vulnerable to a sharp unwind if earnings or geopolitics surprise.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: High-yield credit spreads (the extra yield junk bonds pay over safe government bonds — wider = more stress) sit at 284bps (as of Jul 28) with investment-grade at 81bps — neither is at an extreme, and the HY/IG ratio is 1.34, indicating credit markets are not flashing recession risk.

Bank lending growth is solid at 6.4% year-over-year (as of mid-July); commercial-paper funding spreads (a short-term corporate borrowing gauge) are just 18bps — companies can still fund themselves cheaply in the short-term market.

Bank reserves held at the Fed total $3,062bn (as of Jul 22) — ample system liquidity; the Fed's overnight reverse repo facility (RRP, cash parked at the Fed overnight) has drained to just $2.6bn (Jul 29), meaning excess cash has moved into productive uses, a healthy sign.

The Treasury's cash account (TGA) holds $829.6bn (Jul 22) — a large buffer that, if spent down, would add liquidity to the system and provide a modest offset to any tightening from the rate-hike risk.

Loan syndication rates at 7.15% (Jul 28) and senior loan officer surveys (SLOOS) show only modest net tightening in C&I lending standards (8.1%) and commercial real estate (2%) as of Q2 — credit availability has not seized up despite the rate backdrop.
